practicalQuestion: How should symptoms, strength, movement quality, and sport-specific running or cutting exposure be combined when deciding whether to advance a collegiate athlete from individual rehabilitation to modified team practice?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate athlete returning after a lower-extremity injury
decisionContext.phase: Individual rehabilitation to modified team participation
decisionContext.outcome: Organize a transparent progress-or-hold decision using several relevant signals
decisionContext.constraints: Signals may be collected on different days; team demands vary; medical decision authority remains with the care team

evidenceConfidence.rationale: No source in the pack tests a rule for combining symptoms, strength, movement quality, and running or cutting exposure into a progress-or-hold decision. The closest evidence is a systematic review that found no standardized return-to-sport criterion, one uncontrolled case series and one case study of staged on-field rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction in male soccer players, and indirect monitoring research in healthy elite players.

dimensions.sourceReview: Mixed. The ACL review, the on-field case series, and the Lisfranc series are full-text screened records. The ACL case study, the heart-rate monitoring study, and the asymmetry digest are legacy records whose summaries were not full-text reviewed.
dimensions.directness: Indirect. The sources describe return-to-sport testing and on-field rehabilitation stages. None evaluates how to weigh several signals at the move from individual rehabilitation to modified team practice.
dimensions.consistency: Broadly consistent that no single test or standard criterion exists. However, there are too few comparable studies to judge whether findings agree.
dimensions.transferability: Low to moderate. Most evidence comes from ACL reconstruction in male professional and amateur soccer players. No source studies collegiate athletes, female athletes, court sports, or most other lower-extremity injuries.

bottomLine.text: The library does not contain evidence on how to combine symptoms, strength, movement quality, and sport-specific exposure into a progression decision. Available sources mostly describe ACL reconstruction in male soccer players. A systematic review found no standardized return-to-sport criterion, and the tests it covered were not followed up for reinjury after clearance. Case reports used staged field progressions, with symptoms and field-based asymmetry informing when phases changed. Treat any combined approach as a local, documented framework for professional judgment, not a validated rule.

actions.title: Option A: Staged field progression with entry criteria
actions.text: One case series used a criteria-based rehabilitation process ending in a 5-stage on-field program. Most followed players returned to competition, and some had ACL reinjury. There was no comparison group, so the series does not show that this structure is better than others.

actions.title: Option B: Test battery with strength and patient-reported outcomes
actions.text: A systematic review found isokinetic strength testing was the most common return test. The authors offered suggested batteries and patient-reported outcome measures, but noted that these need validation. The tests reviewed were not followed for reinjury after clearance.

actions.title: Option C: Field-based monitoring of running mechanics and load response
actions.text: In one professional ACL case, the authors described using GPS-embedded sensors to track step impulse asymmetries that guide phase progression. A study of healthy elite players suggested heart-rate responses to drills may show when a player needs more generic running. Individual models need several weeks of prior data.

actions.title: Document how each signal was weighed
actions.text: The evidence does not test how to combine signals collected on different days. As a professional caution, record each signal with its date and the progress-or-hold rationale so the care team can review it.

monitoring.label: Symptoms
monitoring.text: In one ACL case, transient knee pain delayed the return to running. After surgical Lisfranc repair, most athletes reported some residual pain with sport, so expected symptoms may differ by injury. No source sets a symptom threshold for progression.

monitoring.label: Strength and asymmetry
monitoring.text: Asymmetry results depend on the task and metric used, and they can change in size and direction over time. The tests in the return-to-sport review relied on limb symmetry index or comparisons with other metrics. Interpret a single-day value with caution.

monitoring.label: Field exposure and load response
monitoring.text: Field sensors and heart-rate responses to drills may add sport-specific information. Heart-rate models need individual historical data before they can be used, which may not exist for every returning athlete.

guardrails.text: Progression and clearance decisions stay with the treating clinicians and care team. This brief informs their judgment and does not clear an athlete or set policy.
Do not treat any single test, symmetry value, or threshold as a clearance rule. No standardized criterion exists, and the reviewed tests were not linked to reinjury after clearance.
Do not apply ACL soccer stages or outcomes to other injuries without care-team judgment. Hip and ankle return testing evidence was very limited.

limitations.text: Most direct evidence involves ACL reconstruction in male professional or amateur soccer players. No source studies collegiate athletes, female athletes, or court sports.
The designs are a systematic review, uncontrolled case series, and a single case study. None compares decision strategies or follows outcomes after a combined criterion is applied.
The ACL case study, the heart-rate monitoring study, and the asymmetry digest are legacy library records. The asymmetry evidence comes from a digest abstract of a narrative review.

whatCouldChange.text: Prospective studies linking combined criteria at the move to team practice with later setbacks or reinjury would allow stronger guidance.
Studies in collegiate, female, court-sport, or non-ACL lower-extremity populations would improve transferability.

claims.text: A systematic review of lower-extremity return-to-sport testing concluded that, despite extensive ACL literature, there is no standardized return-to-sport criterion.

evidence.excerpt: Even with the enormous amount of literature that exists regarding ACL injuries and testing there is no standardized criterion

claims.text: In that review, isokinetic dynamometry was the most common return-to-sport test, seen in 73% of studies, while only 6.2% of studies addressed hip pathology and only two addressed ankle injuries.

evidence.excerpt: The most common RTS test was isokinetic dynamometry testing which is seen in 73% of studies. Only 6.2% of studies analyzed RTS for individuals with hip pathology and only two studies analyzed RTS for patients with ankle injuries.

claims.text: The review reported that all included tests used limb symmetry index or were validated against another metric, and none followed athletes after return-to-sport clearance to assess reinjury rates.

evidence.excerpt: all the tests in this search used limb symmetry index or ‘‘validated” the test against another metric (ie. Hop test related to strength,) but none of them followed athletes once given RTS clearance to assess re-injury rates.

claims.text: The review authors suggested knee, hip, and ankle test batteries based on the literature and their own practice, while noting that more research validating individual tests is needed.

evidence.excerpt: we have included suggested test batteries for the knee, hip, and ankle based on current literature and our practice as demonstrated in Figs. 2-4. Note, this is an ever-changing science and more research validating individual tests needs to be performed.

claims.text: The review authors stated that psychological patient-reported outcomes should be used for hip and ankle return testing, as with the knee.

evidence.excerpt: As with the knee, psychological patient reported outcomes should be unitized for both the hip and ankle as well.

claims.text: In a case series of male soccer players after ACL reconstruction who completed a criteria-based rehabilitation process ending in a 5-stage on-field program, 84% of the 97 players with follow-up returned to competition (100% of professionals, 80% of amateurs), and 10% sustained an ACL reinjury.

evidence.excerpt: soccer players with ACLR undergoing a criteria-based rehabilitation process, concluding with a 5-stage OFR program.

Results: A minimum 9-month follow-up was possible for 97 players (97%), with a median time of 2.3 years after ACLR and 84% RTC, with higher rates in professionals (100%) than amateurs (80%). Ten (10%) players sustained an ACL reinjury.

claims.text: In a single professional soccer case after ACL reconstruction, transient episodes of knee pain linked to meniscus surgery delayed the return to running.

evidence.excerpt: In the present case, transient episodes of knee pain (as a consequence of the meniscus surgery) delayed the return to running,

claims.text: The authors of the same case study state that GPS-embedded sensor analytics add sport-specific information on stride mechanics and step impulse asymmetries that can be used to guide phase progression.

evidence.excerpt: invaluable sport-specific information to monitor stride mechanics and step impulse asymmetries throughout the rehabilitation process, that can be used to guide phase progression

claims.text: In a study of 10 elite soccer players, the authors suggested that the gap between predicted and actual heart rate during drills could help show when a player needs more generic running conditioning, for example after an injury, and stressed treating each player individually when modeling training response.

evidence.excerpt: HRΔ could provide key information for practitioners to better understand when a player needs more generic running conditioning (e.g. during early pre-season or after an injury)
As such, it is important for each player to be treated individually when building models examining the training response.

claims.text: The heart-rate monitoring approach cannot be used for players with limited historical data and needs at least 60 data points, about 6 to 8 weeks, to build an individual model.

evidence.excerpt: the present monitoring approach can’t be used with players with only limited historical data (e.g., for new signings some time to build the models is needed (≥ 60 data points,27 ~ 6-8 weeks).

claims.text: A digest abstract of a narrative review reported that bilateral asymmetry assessments are task-, metric-, individual-, and sport-specific and fluctuate over time in magnitude and direction.

evidence.excerpt: Assessments of bilateral asymmetries are highly task-, metric-, individual-, and sport-specific; fluctuate significantly in time (in magnitude and, more importantly, in direction);

claims.text: In a retrospective case series of athletes after surgical repair of ligamentous Lisfranc injuries, athletes reported 87% of previous function, and most experienced some residual pain with their sport.

evidence.excerpt: 87% of their previous function. However, the majority of the patients also experienced some residual pain with their respective sport.

assumptions: The specific lower-extremity injury was not stated, so ACL reconstruction evidence was used as the most available proxy, with transferability limits noted.
Modified team practice was treated as roughly equivalent to the late on-field rehabilitation and return-to-training transition described in the soccer sources.
coverageGaps: No evidence on how to weight or combine symptoms, strength, movement quality, and running or cutting exposure into one progress-or-hold decision.
No evidence on handling signals collected on different days or reconciling conflicting signals.
No criteria specific to the transition from individual rehabilitation to modified team practice.
No studies in collegiate athletes, female athletes, or court sports.
Little or no return-testing evidence for hip, ankle, muscle, or other non-ACL lower-extremity injuries.

Potentially relevant leads without accessible text: libraryId 591 (control-chaos continuum for return to sport load planning) and libraryId 578 (dual-task training in musculoskeletal injury rehabilitation).
